title: Ajahn Funn: Now contemplate: we say we have come far from home, from the city. Think about it – it's not far. It's right here…
content:
Home and City Are Right Here in the Heart – Solve Everything at the Heart

Now contemplate: we say we have come far from home, from the city. Think about it – it's not far. It's right here in our own heart. Home, city, everything – it's all right here in our heart. Therefore, the Buddha taught to solve everything at the heart. When the heart has nothing, then everything ends. This point you should often contemplate. Where is our refuge, our dwelling, our support? Why are we suffering and struggling, having to complain? Things themselves don't suffer or struggle. It's only hard on the heart – we say we are poor. Things aren't poor. It's only poor in the heart. Not poor anywhere else.

When the heart is poor, then everything is poor. Wealth and possessions are like that.

If our heart is not poor, then nothing is poor. If the heart does not suffer, then nothing suffers. If the heart is not in difficulty, then nothing is difficult. That's how it is. What difficulty do things have? They don't say anything. They don't suffer or have any difficulty. They all remain neutral. Money and gold don't tell us to go take them. They don't tell us to go seek them.

title: Ajahn Funn: He was courageous and fearless in setting out the religion—about merit, about evil, about everything—because he knew everything, all knowable things, thoroughly and…
content:
Don’t Be Worried or Possessive; Place Your Heart in Buddho

He was courageous and fearless in setting out the religion—about merit, about evil, about everything—because he knew everything, all knowable things, thoroughly and throughout. Nobody taught these things to him. He awakened to them on his own. That’s why he’s called sayambhū—he was self-awakened.

Do you understand yet? Do you understand? I’m teaching these things for you to listen to. Don’t keep on being worried or concerned about this, that, or the other thing. Your worries are a waste of time. They’re fruitless. Throw them all away. Don’t be worried about this, possessive of that. If you place your heart with this or that, you suffer. If you place it here, it doesn’t suffer. So place it with Buddho—awareness itself—and it won’t suffer. Understand?

title: Ajahn Funn: Greed much, often lose gain; Want much, become unable. Want to eat much, get but a pinky's share; Want to eat little, get…
content:
Greed Leads to Ruin: Want Much, Get Little

Greed much, often lose gain; Want much, become unable. Want to eat much, get but a pinky's share; Want to eat little, get a thumb's share.

Now, all of you, reflect on this. Greed leads to ruin. We often want many things, so we end up not getting anything. Why is it that those who want to eat much get only as much as a pinky? Those who want to eat little get as much as a thumb? Which is bigger, the pinky or the thumb? Why is it the reverse? Those who say they want much end up getting only as little as a pinky, while those who are content with little get much. This is how it is for those who are extremely greedy.

Do we want to be ruined? Do we all desire ruin? If so, then be very greedy, very angry, very deluded. Because greed, anger, and delusion are fires. Greed is a fire, anger is a fire, delusion is a fire. Each of these fires burns beings, causing them distress, suffering, and torment. Beings are ruined because of the fires of lobha (greed), dosa (anger), and moha (delusion). This is nothing far away. All of you, reflect so that you know and understand.

title: Ajahn Funn: We have to practice. If you just know about the practice without being experienced in the practice, it’s not good enough. If you’re…
content:
From Knowing to Experienced to Skilled to Intelligent

We have to practice. If you just know about the practice without being experienced in the practice, it’s not good enough. If you’re experienced but not skilled, it’s not good enough. If you’re skilled but not intelligent, it’s not good enough. From knowing you have to become experienced. From being experienced, you have to become skilled. From skilled, you have to become intelligent in how to practice. That’s when it’s up to standard.

If you simply know about these things—knowing about how to ordain, knowing about the precepts, knowing about meditation—but you’re not experienced, or if you’re experienced but not skilled—skilled in getting the mind to enter concentration or in how to contemplate—then you’re not up to standard.

Once you’re skilled, you have to be intelligent. Intelligent in what way? As soon as you focus on the body, if you think of it falling apart, you can immediately see it fall apart. If you think of it disintegrating, you can immediately see it disintegrate. You have that level of strength.

title: Ajahn Funn: Therefore, we undertake the precepts. The Buddha said: pāṇā tipi veramaṇī, adinnā tipi veramaṇī, kāmesu micchācārā tipi veramaṇī, musāvādā tipi veramaṇī, surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā tipi…
content:
Abstaining from Killing, Stealing, Sexual Misconduct, Lying, Intoxicants Brings Peace

Therefore, we undertake the precepts. The Buddha said: pāṇā tipi veramaṇī, adinnā tipi veramaṇī, kāmesu micchācārā tipi veramaṇī, musāvādā tipi veramaṇī, surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā tipi veramaṇī. Veramaṇī means to abstain. If we all abstain from these five faults, then we are at ease. Wherever we go, we are at ease. Sitting is easy, sleeping is easy, walking is easy, standing is easy – because we don’t have these five faults. The suffering and difficulty we have now are because of these five faults. Why say that? Because we fear being killed, we fear being robbed, we fear sexual misconduct from others, we fear false speech, we fear intoxicated people. That’s what we fear. If these five things were absent, our towns and our country would prosper.

Because there is no killing – even a red ant or a tiny insect, the Buddha taught not to kill. They love life; we love life. If we don’t do it, why would anyone kill another person? If we don’t have these things, then all those faults disappear. If we kill others, later they will kill us – we will be born with short lives, die young, die in childhood, be separated from loved ones, or contract diseases and dangers. We don’t want that. Since we don’t want it, we should abstain from pāṇātipāta (killing). That’s how it is.

title: Ajahn Funn: This is samucchedapahāna — abandonment by cutting off. This is samucchedavirati — abstinence by cutting off. It rejects everything. It does not acknowledge…
content:
Turning Off the Receiver: Not Acknowledging, Not Accepting

This is samucchedapahāna — abandonment by cutting off. This is samucchedavirati — abstinence by cutting off. It rejects everything. It does not acknowledge or receive any of them. Right now, it acknowledges everything. When suffering arises, it acknowledges “suffering.” When hardship arises, it acknowledges “hardship.” When good arises, it acknowledges “I am good.” When evil arises, it acknowledges “I am evil.” When love arises, it acknowledges “I love.” When hatred arises, it acknowledges “I hate.” It goes on acknowledging like that, and that is suffering. So let go. Contemplate only inwardly. Do not acknowledge. Then things do not come to us. If we have no receiver, nothing enters. It’s like broadcasting a radio signal as much as you like: if we have no receiver, it’s silent. Nothing reaches us at all. If we have a receiver, then it reaches us. Turn off the receiver. Don’t accept. Then it cannot enter. Not going out, not receiving in, it remains independent. It stays alone by itself. Ekodhammo — the one Dhamma. Ekaṅ cittaṅ — the one mind. Having the mind as one. Eko dhammo — the Dhamma is one. Being one, it is supreme. Eko itthiyo — woman is supreme; eko puriso — man is supreme. It is not shaken by anything. Having become supreme — that’s the greatness right there.

title: Ajahn Funn: In the Ovāda Pātimokkha, the Buddha said: "Sabbapāpassa akaraṇaṃ, kusalassūpasampadā, sacittapariyodapanaṃ — etaṃ buddhāna sāsanaṃ." If we interpret the meaning in our own…
content:
The Teaching of the Buddhas: Abstain from Evil, Undertake Good, Purify the Mind

In the Ovāda Pātimokkha, the Buddha said: "Sabbapāpassa akaraṇaṃ, kusalassūpasampadā, sacittapariyodapanaṃ — etaṃ buddhāna sāsanaṃ." If we interpret the meaning in our own language: "Abstain from all evil" — abandon evil in body, speech, and mind. Whatever is evil, abandon; whatever is not good or beautiful, abandon — do not do it, whether by body, speech, or mind.

Then, kusalassūpasampadā — undertake wholesome actions, make merit, bring about goodness in body and mind; perform virtuous deeds. Sacittapariyodapanaṃ — purify the mind, make it clear and bright. The Buddha said "purify the mind," not anything else. The mind becomes clear. Etaṃ buddhāna sāsanaṃ — this is the teaching of the Buddhas. The Buddha did not tell us to abandon evil elsewhere — just from body and mind. That is all. Happiness and suffering do not come from elsewhere; they arise within our own body.

Therefore, it is said: listen to what is within. In our practice, if we only look outside, only listen outside, we will not see, or we will see but cannot abandon or let go. For example, birth: we see people being born; we see people aging; but we cannot let go. We see sickness and disease; but we cannot let go. We see people dying; but we cannot let go.

title: Ajahn Funn: When knowledge is lacking, we cannot find a refuge. In the Saccakiriyā Gāthā it is said: Natthi me saraṇaṃ aññaṃ – "I have…
content:
Natthi Me Saraṇaṃ Aññaṃ: I Have No Other Refuge

When knowledge is lacking, we cannot find a refuge. In the Saccakiriyā Gāthā it is said: Natthi me saraṇaṃ aññaṃ – "I have no other refuge." Relying on this or that, nothing can be relied upon; even our own self cannot be relied upon. Ordinary people, the country, the nation cannot be relied upon. Father, mother, grandparents, ancestors – none can be relied upon. Even ourselves cannot be relied upon. What then is our refuge? Buddho me saraṇaṃ varaṃ – "The Buddha is my excellent refuge." Bring it inside and look: where is the Buddha right now?

Opanayiko – bring inside. Buddha means the knower. Consider: where is it right now? Buddho, buddho – it is within the mind. Buddho means knowing one's own mind as the knower. Lacking knowledge alone, there is no refuge at all. It is like a dead person. A dead person lacks knowledge; they cannot do a single thing. That is why we have come to remind our minds to have a refuge, a place of homage, of worship. Do not doubt or hesitate.

title: Ajahn Funn: Regarding bang-sukun, there is an ancient story. In the suttas, it is said that there was a beautiful woman named Sirimā. The monks…
content:
The Sirimā Story: Contemplating a Corpse Leads to Arahantship

Regarding bang-sukun, there is an ancient story. In the suttas, it is said that there was a beautiful woman named Sirimā. The monks who were still ordinary worldlings (puthujjana), when they saw her beauty, felt lust, desire, and delight to the point that they could not even go for alms. Because of their lust and delight in that form. Later, that woman died, her khandhas ceased. The Buddha used an expedient means: he sent people to invite those monks to contemplate, as explained above.

Bhavobhavā aniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ, anattā – all states of becoming are impermanent. They are just a pool of pus and lymph, like this.

Imaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ bhaveti – one must develop meditation by contemplating this. Who would want a form like this? Even if given away for free, who would want it? When those monks went and saw, they felt a sense of spiritual urgency, their minds became calm, and they all attained arahantship. That's how it was.

Therefore, contemplating a corpse has great benefits. That is why monks are invited to perform bang-sukun. But if monks accept the invitation and then go and focus on getting money and gold, that won't work. Huh. It becomes like that. The teachers advise to reflect on kammaṭṭhāna, to contemplate in order to gain great benefits.

title: Ajahn Funn: Right now, our bodily kamma is calm. Our verbal kamma has ceased. Only mental kamma remains. Mental kamma is the act of inclining…
content:
Good Kamma Is a Calm Mind – Bad Kamma Is a Chaotic Mind

Right now, our bodily kamma is calm. Our verbal kamma has ceased. Only mental kamma remains. Mental kamma is the act of inclining and thinking. Whatever kamma we have thought – whether merit or demerit – that kamma is here. Recall this: Kammassakomhi – kamma is my own possession. Kalyāṇaṃ vā pāpakaṃ vā tassa dāyādā bhavissanti – whatever kamma I have done, whether good or bad, I will inherit its result. We must know this. What is good kamma? In short, it is a calm mind, a good mind, with happiness and comfort. That is called good kamma.

And bad kamma (pāpakaṃ)? What is it? It is an unwholesome mind – suffering, chaotic, distressed. That is bad kamma, and we will receive its results in turn.

When you know that something is not good, abandon it. Here we are, old kamma not yet exhausted, and new kamma keeps adding on. Will it ever run out? Stop it. There is no other way to cleanse oneself of demerit and kamma except by sitting in meditation. When our mind is calm, there is no kamma. Where would kamma come from?
